newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan stocks seen as surprise performer in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan stocks seen as surprise performer in Asia.

text.p: Pakistan's stock market could be a surprise performer in 1997 if the economy responds to Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's reforms, a research report said on Monday.

"With the political outlook substantially improved, corporate fundamentals intact and earnings growth momentum on the rise...Pakistan is likely to be the surprise outperformer in Asia in 1997," said International Asset Management Company Ltd (IAMC) in its quarterly investment report.

The IAMC, an adviser to the Morgan Stanley Pakistan Investment Fund, said it had continued to build its core holding because the Pakistan market looked promising, with potential year-on-year returns in excess of 40 percent in calendar 1997.
IAMC analysts estimated that year-on-year earnings for the stock market were minus 10.5 percent in 1996.
The report said the government's tax and tariff cuts would lift company earnings in the next two years.
"The Karachi Stock Exchange 100 companies' earnings growth will be pushed up between four to six percent over the current estimates of 22 percent for 1997/98 (July-June)."
The Pakistani market rose 18 percent in the first quarter of this year.

Political instability and weak economic fundamentals hurt local stocks in 1996. The index finished the year at 1,339.93, down 515.29 points or 27.8 percent from the year's high of 1,855.22 on February 15.
The Karachi 100-share index fell 8.71 points or 0.57 percent to 1,528.80 at noon on Monday from the previous close.

"Pakistan's continued political instability was a major problem...but there has been a sea-change after a pro-business Nawaz Sharif government came to power with an absolute majority in February," said Nadeem Naqvi, research head at IAMC.
"Sharif's economic reforms have a real chance of being implemented, which is the most significant factor," he said.
The report said the government had moved swiftly to tackle economic problems, with plans to revamp the tax collection system, introduce new banking laws and crack down on corruption.

Sharif unveiled his reform package on March 28, shortly after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) halted a standby loan to Pakistan when it became clear the country would not meet its fiscal targets. The IMF has tentatively agreed to start talks on a new medium-term loan later this year.

"Over the next 12 to 18 months, the effects of the announced reforms (in) boosting exports...and prospective direct foreign investment should lead to a significant revival of growth," the report said.
"If the (1997/98) budget focuses on growth alongside greater fiscal discipline...1997 will witness a gradual reduction in uncertainty on the economic front," it said.

The new budget, due in June, is likely to incorporate demand-side policies to control current spending and meet key IMF economic targets to qualify for a medium-term loan under the fund's enhanced structural adjustment facility in 1997/98, the report said.
The IAMC said the Karachi index would range from 1,500 to 1,650 points in the second quarter because foreign investors were awaiting a positive IMF signal.
They also wanted to see how foreign exchange reserves fared after June debt repayments. Local institutions would remain sellers at levels above 1,650 points.
